entry.title: Reality Check: Why ‘You Can See Everything’ Faces a Long Road to the Oscars
entry.summary: 'You Can See Everything' is a box office sensation. History and math tell us that probably won't lead to Oscars glory.
entry.content:
Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”

Everybody’s talking about the A24 documentary “You Can See Everything,” and many Oscar prognosticators are jumping on board the Best Picture bandwagon. Don’t buy the hype.

While there’s a lot to admire about Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s entertaining nonfiction approach to parsing the distorted reality of disgraced Thanatos founder Elizabeth Holmes just before she went to prison, it’s still a long road for a surprise box-office documentary hit ($45 million domestic and counting) to garner enough Oscar votes for a Best Picture nomination.

Related Stories
Barbara Barrie, Oscar-Nominated ‘Breaking Away’ and ‘Private Benjamin’ Star, Dies at 95
A Flop at the Chinese Box Office Shows AI Still Has a Tough Road Ahead in Theaters

The folks who believe it’s possible are listening to the current buzz and noise, much of it from younger movie fans on social media, and the film‘s undeniable heat. A24’s brilliant “no spoilers” marketing campaign has pushed more moviegoers than usual into theaters early in the run. But the Academy membership is still senior-centric.

Here are the necessary steps for A24 to nab a BP nod.

Step One: Critic group wins. This week’s Gotham nomination for Best Documentary Feature is a start. The movie needs to land awards from the NYFCC, LAFCA, and NSFC. The Golden Globes will be no help, as they do not give a documentary prize. Critic support will add prestige and convince laggards to watch the movie on the Academy portal.

Step Two: Lure international voters. “YCSE” is an American movie, even if it confronts alternate reality issues familiar to everyone. It has yet to open overseas. Recognition from the European Film Awards or BAFTAs would show support outside North America. (Checking on eligibility)

Step Three: Legitimize the movie with the 750-member documentary branch, which is notorious for rejecting popular nonfiction like Morgan Neville’s “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?” and Brett Morgen’s “Jane.” Some doc voters harbor strong opinions about reenactments, which YCSE leans into in the second half. There’s a strong chance the doc branch will not nominate this movie.

Step Four: Figure Out Nathan Fielder. The offbeat, deliberately awkward creator behind TV series “The Rehearsal” and “The Curse” is an acquired taste. He’s been doing some press interviews and panels, but full-court glad-handing may not be his strong suit.

Step Five: Break out of the doc box. In the Oscars‘ 98-year history, no documentary has ever been nominated for Best Picture. Over the past two decades, none of the docs that have succeeded at the box office have made it, not even Michael Moore’s 2004 Palme d’Or winner “Fahrenheit 9/11” — which was ineligible for the Oscar because it played on TV before the contentious national election. Moore received two documentary Oscar nominations for “Sicko” and “Bowling for Columbine,” winning the prize for the latter.

Step Six: Beat out the A24 competition. Four movies are vying for Best Picture this year from A24. The distributor is also pushing Olivia Wilde’s four-hander “The Invite,” Jesse Eisenberg’s crowdpleaser “The Debut,” and rookie Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” (a more likely Original Screenplay nod). “No one has the bandwidth to do every film justice,” said one Oscar campaigner. “It’s hard for a studio to get more than two.”

Step Seven: Woo the actors. With more than 1,100 voters, the actors are the dominant branch in the Academy. On GoldDerby.com, Experts list Amanda Seyfried in the sixth spot as a Supporting Actor contender. (The movie is ranked eighth for Best Picture.) In “YCSE,” she performs transcripts as Elizabeth Holmes in various reenactments, whom she played in the TV series “The Dropout.” And she plays herself. This is a hard one to call. Many believe this is more about A24 hype than reality.

Step Eight: Do the Numbers. Look at branches of the Academy and count the ones that are likely to vote for this movie. The classic way of figuring out a Best Picture contender is to see where its support lies among the active 10,365 voters. That’s how I figured out that “F1” might make it to Best Picture last year. Some of the 750 documentary branch members will vote for “YCSE” and are the most likely to see the movie. Anyone can vote for Best Picture, but the doc is unlikely to win any craft nominations: animation (729), casting directors (191), cinematographers (326), costume designers (205), editors (421), hair & makeup (225), music (430), production design (446), production and technology (424, they don’t have a branch but they vote), short films (234), sound (575), and visual effects (679). More likely to vote for the movie are such non-crafts as artists representatives (266), directors (587), executives (770), marketing and public relations (672), producers (692), and writers (534). The movie has no script per se. But writers may appreciate its ingenious structure and evolution.

Finally, if “YCSE” were to become the first doc to score a Best Picture slot, it would likely do so without any other nominations.

entry.title: Barbara Barrie, Oscar-Nominated ‘Breaking Away’ and ‘Private Benjamin’ Star, Dies at 95
entry.summary: Barbara Barrie, the Oscar-nominated star of 'Breaking Away,' 'Barney Miller,' and 'Private Benjamin' had died at 95.
entry.content:
Barbara Barrie, a character actress best known for playing boisterous moms in “Breaking Away” and “Private Benjamin,” has died. She was 95.

Barrie’s daughter, Jane Harnick, told the New York Times that her mother had terminal cancer and said her death was “medically assisted.”

Barrie was an inveterate scene stealer who was a frequent presence on stage and screen. On Broadway, she appeared in the original cast of Stephen Sondheim’s “Company,” a revolutionary musical that examined relationships and commitment. Barrie earned a Tony Award nomination for her role in the 1970 production. Other Broadway credits included Neil Simon’s hit “California Suite.”

For her film work, Barrie won the best actress prize at the 1964 Cannes Film Festival for “One Potato, Two Potato,” an interracial romance, in which her character confronts prejudice while falling in love with a Black man. But it was “Breaking Away,” and her work as the blue-collar mother of a cycling enthusiast, that put Barrie on the map. She was nominated for best supporting sctress for the 1979 coming-of-age classic, then reprised the part in a 1980 TV series based on “Breaking Away,” earning an Emmy nomination.

Barrie also was known to audiences for her turn on the 1970s detective sitcom “Barney Miller,” portraying the wife of the title character. Other credits included the films “Judy Berlin,” “The Bell Jar,” and Disney’s “Hercules,” as well as appearances on “Law & Order” and “Suddenly Susan.”

Barrie was a published author. She wrote children’s books, as well as “Second Act” and “Don’t Die of Embarrassment,” which examined her battle with colorectal cancer.

entry.title: A Flop at the Chinese Box Office Shows AI Still Has a Tough Road Ahead in Theaters
entry.summary: A fully AI generated feature, 'Sanxingdui: Future Past,' flopped at the Chinese box office this past weekend, earning just $181,000.
entry.content:
One of the old adages of the film business was that people wouldn’t pay to watch an actor in theaters if they could see them for free on TV. Today, AI-generated content in China is ubiquitous, with a recent report suggesting that among the explosion of microdramas in China, nearly two-thirds of those videos are all generated by AI.

But it seems there’s a big difference between what audiences, even Chinese ones, will pay to buy a ticket for compared to what they will consume on their phones for free.

This past weekend, a fully, AI-generated feature film titled “Sanxingdui: Future Past” opened in Chinese theaters and grossed just RMB1.21 million, which is about $181,000, according to the film’s producer Bona Film Group. It’s the first AI feature to get the right to play on Chinese screens, and it makes it a big flop, as Bona in a recent blog post said the budget for the movie was 10 million yuan, which is about $1.5 million.

Related Stories
Hoorae’s Microdramas Found 580 Million Views. Can TikTok Get Hollywood Working Again? — Watch
What Do You Get When the ‘Texas Chainsaw’ Director Takes on the Marquis de Sade? The Kinky Pleasures of ‘Night Terrors’

That’s about the budget of a small indie, and perhaps more than you would’ve guessed when so much of the narrative around AI is that it’s going to cut costs and that you can make “Avatar” for next to nothing. But Bona says the film was produced over the course of two years from a team of 70 to 80 people, and some of the creators bristled at the idea that the images were created with a single click. In fact, the blog post says “Future Past” was being tweaked and technically still “shooting” up until a week before the film hit theaters.

Clearly, though, that level of artistry wasn’t evident on screen. An attendee told the international outlet AFP that the AI still “falls short” of a human-made, live-action production. “In the future, just like films, maybe decades later, it would get to a level when people are all willing to pay to watch,” she told AFP. “But for the moment, I think there would be very few who would.”

Bona had reason to believe that the film could attract a reasonable audience in theaters. “Sanxingdui: Future Past” originated as an AI microdrama series itself that managed nearly 200 million views. In fact, production has already begun on Bona’s second AI-generated feature, “Unplanned Operation in the Cold Moon,” and that the company has received requests to screen the movie in other countries outside of China.

The challenge though of releasing a 100-minute feature compared to a microdrama that could be just a few minutes in length is that it has to go through a content review process before it can be screened in theaters, so that speed to bring something new and fresh to market wasn’t there for “Sanxingdui.”

All of this will be something that the upcoming film from YouTuber and AI creator Gossip Goblin will be watching closely. His fully AI feature, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” is opening in U.S. theaters this December and is even launching international sales at the American Film Market next month. It’s the first such movie to receive a rating from the MPA, and it’s even intending to submit for eligibility at the Oscars for Best Animated Feature. Gossip Goblin has a large audience that he cultivates across numerous psychedelic, sprawling AI shorts, many of which belong to a connected story universe, so he’s hoping to emulate the Markiplier and “Iron Lung” playbook to draw a dedicated fanbase to theaters via a self-releasing strategy.

But whether it’s in China or America, people go to the theaters expecting a certain level of cinematic quality above what they can get at home on their phones. We’ll see if the “Sanxingdui” experiment ends up translating to American audiences.

entry.title: Hoorae’s Microdramas Found 580 Million Views. Can TikTok Get Hollywood Working Again? — Watch
entry.summary: Watch executives from Hoorae Media discuss their breakout hit 'Screen Time' and the future of microdramas at IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Summit.
entry.content:
The couples have secrets(!). The TV has been hijacked(!!). And somewhere between the next confession and its immediate cliffhanger(!!!), Issa Rae’s Hoorae Media is trying to figure out how to get Hollywood back to work. In “Screen Time,” the production company’s first microdrama, released on TikTok earlier this year, a double date becomes a waking nightmare when a sinister figure takes over one couple’s living room TV screen and demands the lovers come clean(?!)… or risk exposure.

For the people who made the juicy series, the stakes are less lurid but plenty urgent: Can a thriller told in minute-long segments sustain a business that keeps indie filmmakers, cast, and crew on set? So far, there’s reason to keep watching and, more encouragingly, to keep experimenting.

Related Stories
What Do You Get When the ‘Texas Chainsaw’ Director Takes on the Marquis de Sade? The Kinky Pleasures of ‘Night Terrors’
Slamdance Names Screenplay Competition Winners for 2026 — Read the Full List

By the time Hoorae executives Jax Clark and Dzifa Yador joined IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit on Saturday, October 17, “Screen Time” had accumulated nearly 580 million views across TikTok and its dedicated microdrama app, PineDrama.

“My favorite comment is, ‘Who put Netflix on my TikTok?’” Yador said. “It just really validated the fact that we did not abandon what it takes to build a premium product.” 580 million views is a lot of attention, by any standard. Whether that attention can sustain the people making microdramas is the question behind Hoorae’s developing business — and in a room full of eager film folks ready to roll up their sleeves, Clark and Yador made an appealingly practical case for finding out where bite-sized verticals can take their company and collaborators.

“How are we creating a sustainable pipeline that can bring new talent, new voices, new points of view into the industry?” Clark said. “As barriers to entry continue to get higher and the industry constricts and budgets are constrained, that’s continued to be an internal mission and engine for the company.”

Before bringing “Insecure” to HBO, Rae had already built an audience on YouTube with “The Mis-Adventures of Awkward Black Girl.” Hoorae’s microdrama effort returns to those digital roots through its TikTok distribution model, openly embraced brand partnerships, and a willingness to rethink what a day’s work — and even a story’s eventual audience — might look like.

“Obviously we work in television, we work in film, and now to be back in digital, which is where Issa really got her start and started building her audience has felt like a very beautiful full circle moment,” Clark said. (Notably, fellow summit speaker and inaugural Future of Filmmaking Award honoree Curry Barker knows something about that online runway: His reported $800 YouTube feature “Milk & Serial” preceded his theatrical breakout with “Obsession.”)

For Yador, the challenge was adapting Hoorae’s storytelling to the digital world’s existing habits.

“It wasn’t about trying to reimagine what storytelling is because we do that so well already,” she said. “Kudos to Jax and Issa and the entire team, but it was about how do we repackage it for the now, understanding where people are spending the most of their time on phones and how to continue to elevate the space so that it feels very much like a Hoorae product.”

Clark further described Hoorae’s ambitions as extending to creatives stuck in industry assistant jobs or “whatever writer purgatory they’re in,” with productions offering experience on set and in post. Anyone hoping to rescue an unproduced screenplay by rotating it 90 degrees should temper their expectations, she said. But if you’re willing to adapt to the microdrama world, there’s real opportunity.

“This isn’t a format where it’s like, ‘Hey, I have a feature script that no one invested in and now I’m just going to chop it up into minutes and we can make this a microdrama,’” Clark said. “It’s not an apples to apples conversion that happens. Part of it is talking to creatives who are willing to try something new and build something that maintains the integrity of the medium.”

Surely, though, anyone with a phone and a flair for betrayal could give it a shot, right? Maybe.

Yador said Hoorae spent two years studying vertical storytelling before diving into the space, and they don’t regret the prep. With “Screen Time,” Clark said, the central question was familiar to anyone who enjoys a good erotic thriller: “Can you really trust the person you go to sleep with every night?” But to make that hook work specifically for vertical, Hoorae assembled a team combining traditional filmmaking experience with unique expertise relevant excelling in the microdrama format.

“We have a blend of just talented filmmakers, but then we also have the top of the class in terms of people who have done verticals before,” Yador said. “We feel really confident working with actors who maybe haven’t done this before because we know we have the team to help educate them.

Amusingly, for cast members already accustomed to verticals, an assignment from Hoorae can actually mean dialing things down: “It’s actors who are maybe used to coming out on a hundred for every scene and we can tell them, actually we can ground this and we want you to try something new here and maybe play this more seriously and maybe riff a little bit,” Clark said.

Legibility is key, and even a carefully considered character arc has to survive the instability of a scrollable feed. After all, a viewer might meet these people in the finale and need to watch in reverse.

“Wherever you get dropped in has to feel just as propulsive and just as noteworthy as your pilot episode and sticky enough to keep you in there,” Yador explained. “And there’s kind of a machine in terms of the mechanics of how you develop a microdrama. And those are the engines that we’re talking about and they exist even in the finale.”

TikTok helps Hoorae navigate that unpredictability. Yador credited the platform with joining as a distribution partner as “Screen Time” production was wrapping, and with providing insights into what attracts viewers. The partnership, announced in April, provides exclusive distribution on TikTok and PineDrama, with Hoorae’s shows available for free with ad support.

That backing matters for filmmakers wondering whether they could follow suit. Hoorae has Rae’s reputation, a talent network, and a platform partner — while uploading your own thriller and waiting for the algorithm to fall in love is a different proposition. Still, for this pioneering and hopeful group the relationship has already supported an expanding slate. Following “Screen Time” came “The Compatibility Experiment,” about a couple testing their relationship on a reality dating show, and “Parental Advisory,” which brings affairs, rivalries, and potential murder to the PTA.

“We didn’t want to just try to do exactly what everyone else was doing or what other people were projecting would work,” Clark said. With 10 more microdramas in the works for next year, there should be plenty of secrets to go around. But who pays to keep the confessions coming?

There is serious money in microdramas, although it often comes from asking viewers to pay for the next revelation. Omdia forecasts $1.5 billion in U.S. microdrama revenue in 2026, while its earlier global research found more than 60 percent of revenue came from subscriptions or transactional payments. Hoorae’s approach requires a different calculation, and asked what 580 million views had done for Hoorae financially, Yador described developing relationships instead of revenue.

“It’s important to us that the brands feel integrated into the content rather than it just being slapped on and then you just call it branded content,” Yador said, adding that Hoorae’s in-house sales team seeks brands willing to protect the creative, getting specific about who should hold a product and why. “We’re quite intentional about how we’re engaging with brands that way. And so I think to the consumer lens of it, I think it feels natural and tasteful rather than on the nose branded content.”

Clark said digital production also allows closer collaboration with advertisers than film and television projects involving more partners. “It’s actually been pretty fun building story and these relationships at the same time in a way that also is constantly feeding the financial model in a way that can make sense,” she said. How consistent that model really remains unclear, but Hoorae is enthusiastic.

“This is a volume game,” Yador said. “’How much can you make in X amount of time with X budget?’ — is always a math equation that we’re trying to solve for that feels very one-to-one with just kind of vertical universally. For an industry still contending with declining production in Los Angeles, the prospect of more work is welcome. And what that work pays for matters just as much.

“Screen Time” is a SAG production, with The Wrap reporting on a Verticals Agreement that establishes minimum pay, overtime, and pension and health contributions for Hoorae workerks. Covered productions remain a fraction of the market. And still, Clark and Yador sounded excited to be making things and building profitable artistic environments. As creators, the obstacles were familiar even when the delivery system wasn’t: Find the fans. Make it work. Have we tried a… kiss?

“When we’re on set, we’ve scripted things that this needs to hit, this will drive engagement and it’s not popping,” Clark said, laughing. “So, we’re like, okay, well maybe they need to kiss! Maybe we need a slap! Maybe we need something else here. We’re able to try things in the moment.”

The hope is that those bursts of experimentation can keep adding up to lasting employment at Hoorae. Considering what wanted for the brand’s future, Clark returned to the work: “More TV, more film, more verticals, more people being able to get back to work and sustain themselves on this art.”

Watch the complete panel from our Future of Filmmaking Summit in the video above.

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen. For more information, visit here.

entry.title: What Do You Get When the ‘Texas Chainsaw’ Director Takes on the Marquis de Sade? The Kinky Pleasures of ‘Night Terrors’
entry.summary: The director of 'The Texas Chainsaw Massacre' joined forces with 'Nightmare on Elm Street' star Robert Englund for the 1993 Marquis de Sade adaptation
entry.content:
Director Tobe Hooper is simultaneously one of horror’s most celebrated filmmakers and one of its most underrated — celebrated thanks to his direction of one of the most influential and accomplished horror movies of all time, “The Texas Chainsaw Massacre,” but underrated given the overall lack of appreciation for most of what came after. Credit for Hooper’s biggest hit, “Poltergeist,” is generally (and erroneously) attributed to producer Steven Spielberg. Elsewhere, though Hooper’s TV adaptation of “Salem’s Lot” has gained stature in recent years, he’s generally discussed as a director whose work lives in the shadow of “Chainsaw” — when he’s discussed at all.

Related Stories
Slamdance Names Screenplay Competition Winners for 2026 — Read the Full List
ACE Eddie Awards Will Honor John Carpenter as Filmmaker of the Year

Yet among the more than a dozen features Hooper made after “The Texas Chainsaw Massacre” are several truly distinctive works that often — as in the case of the profoundly melancholy and unsettling 1981 slasher film “The Funhouse” — rank among the best in their horror subgenres. Some of these movies are not only forgotten but were barely known to begin with, given Hooper’s termite-like existence in the 1990s and 2000s, decades spent toiling in low-budget straight-to-DVD indies, and anonymous cable television assignments.

Thankfully, boutique physical media labels like Arrow, Shout! Factory, and Vinegar Syndrome have spent the last several years giving the director’s work the respect it deserves, with supplement-laden 4K UHD and Blu-ray releases of essential Hooper films like “Eaten Alive,” “The Funhouse,” and “The Mangler.” Now, Vinegar Syndrome has produced an exquisite special edition of Hooper’s 1993 riff on the Marquis de Sade, “Night Terrors,” a film that ranks among the filmmaker’s most maligned movies. It’s also one of his best.

That “Night Terrors” is so interesting and so aligned with Hooper’s preoccupations and stylistic motifs is a little surprising, given that it was a for-hire assignment the director came to relatively late in the proceedings. The movie originated with Harry Alan Towers, a producer with, to put it mildly, a colorful past — in the 1960s he was a reputed Soviet spy who operated a vice ring tasked with luring and blackmailing prominent U.S. officials, including President John F. Kennedy.

By the time “Night Terrors” came around, Towers was a producer with dozens of features on his resume, including several Marquis de Sade adaptations. “Night Terrors” began as a reworking of one of these, 1969’s “Eugenie…The Story of Her Journey into Perversion,” but it evolved into something fairly different by the time Towers partnered with Israeli producer Yoram Globus in the early 1990s. The idea was that the Cannon Films impresario, whose long-time partnership with Menahem Golan had recently ended, would join forces with Towers to remake “Eugenie” as a horror picture.

Globus had a past with Hooper, Cannon having financed three of the director’s most well-resourced — and financially unsuccessful — features in the 1980s. After Hooper hit big with “Poltergeist” in 1982, he signed a deal with Cannon that yielded “Lifeforce,” “Invaders From Mars,” and “Texas Chainsaw Massacre 2,” three artistic triumphs but economic disasters that accelerated Cannon’s demise and essentially put an end to Hooper’s career working with generous budgets.

Hooper and Golan-Globus were happy with each other despite the movies’ box-office failures and a bit of executive meddling on the extremely expensive “Lifeforce.” Cannon was, in fact, an extremely filmmaker-friendly outfit despite its reputation as exploitation schlockmeisters. Alongside bread-and-butter lowest common denominator fare like “Breakin 2: Electric Boogaloo” and “Death Wish III,” they financed auteur projects by John Cassavetes (“Love Streams”), Robert Altman (“Fool For Love”), and Jean-Luc Godard (“King Lear”), and granted those directors almost total creative control.

Hooper was no exception, smuggling his usual critique of American culture and values that began with “Chainsaw” into the big-budget “Lifeforce” and “Invaders of Mars” (and the slightly more reasonably budgeted “Chainsaw 2”), without compromising the ferocity of his point of view. In spite of Hooper’s rapport with Globus, however, he was not the original director of “Night Terrors” — that distinction would go to British journeyman Gerry O’Hara.

O’Hara came on board to direct a script by Daniel Matmor that drew on elements from de Sade’s “Philosophy in the Boudoir” and synthesized them into a very 1990s cocktail of horror, softcore pornography, and philosophical inquiry. The movie is framed by material depicting the Marquis de Sade (played by Freddy Krueger himself, Robert Englund) ranting from his prison cell; this is intercut with a present-day story in which Genie (Zoe Trilling), a young American woman visiting Egypt, is indoctrinated into a sex cult led by one of de Sade’s descendants (also played by Englund).

Conflicting reports surround O’Hara’s departure from the project, but one factor seems to be the switch from Egypt to Israel as a shooting location. This change, driven by financial considerations, also troubled Englund, since his primary motivation for signing on was his desire to see Egypt. When they decided to change locations, Globus and Towers had an unhappy star and no director.

They brought on Hooper largely to appease Englund, who had worked with the director on “Eaten Alive” and the pilot episode of “Freddy’s Nightmares” (and would work with him again on “The Mangler”). He was probably happy for the job, given that whatever commercial capital he had accumulated at Cannon after the success of “Poltergeist” was long gone. Hooper had spent the years since 1986’s “Chainsaw 2” largely in television, with only 1990’s “Spontaneous Combustion” appearing in theaters since.

The director’s late arrival to “Night Terrors” doesn’t show anywhere in the film, which feels like pure, undiluted Hooper; it’s a glorious showcase for his gifts, from the abundantly horrific imagery in de Sade’s imprisonment and torture to the dark, ironic sense of humor that characterizes the scenes depicting the sex cult (scenes that are both funnier and more disturbing in the age of Jeffrey Epstein). Coming in to save the day in the late innings rather than having labored over the project for months or years, Hooper feels liberated in “Night Terrors,” and lets his imagination run wild.

The erotic elements of “Night Terrors” in particular are really something to behold, from a snake-fellating belly dancer and naked horseback riding to the sex party whose guests arrive dressed as children. Hooper has always been marked by his transgressive side, whether in violence, sex, or politics. His films are provocations, and “Night Terrors” is no exception. He’s also always been marked by his sly and aggressive sense of humor, which is put to good use here — in fact, the line between erotic, offensive, and hilarious is often blurred to extremely entertaining effect, as Hooper pushes the outrageousness of Matmor’s script to its limit and beyond.

He also takes his usual sense of intertextual commentary in new directions thanks to the movie’s sexual component. Hooper was always the kind of director, like many of his peers, who was comfortable with referencing other movies and using those references in conversation with his own work to create new meanings. The kids in “Salem’s Lot,” “Poltergeist,” and “Invaders From Mars” all live in shrines to pop culture that inform and reflect their own lives, and even the killer in “The Funhouse” has a special relationship with Frankenstein’s monster.

In “Night Terrors,” Hooper creates a dialogue not only with other horror movies, but with the erotic films and TV shows that proliferated in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The story of Genie’s sexual awakening has more than a little in common with Zalman King-scripted soft-core fare like “9 1/2 Weeks,” “Two Moon Junction,” and “Red Shoe Diaries,” and Hooper borrows the highly diffused neon lighting and ad agency-inspired aesthetic of those works for his own sex scenes. Yet he also constantly undercuts or plays against them with satire, gore, and just out-and-out weirdness — it’s hard for a soft-core movie to enter the nervous system unimpeded when it’s punctuated with eyeball-gouging and Robert Englund theatrically pontificating while hanging from a cross.

In spite of — or perhaps because of — the everything and the kitchen sink maximalism of Hooper’s approach, “Night Terrors” remains one of his most poorly received films, with a lower IMDb ranking even than 2000’s excoriated “Crocodile” and barely any mention at all in “American Twilight,” the definitive and indispensable text on Hooper’s work. This makes Vinegar Syndrome’s Blu-ray release invaluable, as they’ve meticulously restored the film from an archival print and loaded it with respectful, informative extras. It’s a great way to discover Hooper’s most unfairly neglected film, and to ponder the breadth and depth of his work in general.

The limited edition Blu-ray of Tobe Hooper‘s “Night Terrors” is now available from Vinegar Syndrome.

entry.title: Slamdance Names Screenplay Competition Winners for 2026 — Read the Full List
entry.summary: Slamdance announces its 2026 screenplay competition winners, with James Oxyer’s 'Termite' taking the $10,000 grand prize. Read the full list.
entry.content:
A stranger hiding inside the walls is just the beginning of the trouble in this year’s Slamdance screenplay competition grand prize winner. IndieWire can exclusively announce that James Oxyer’s “Termite” has earned the contest’s top accolade, with a story about a lonely teenager whose unexpected houseguest sets the stage for an increasingly fraught drama.

AGBO hosted the 2026 winners at an awards ceremony in downtown Los Angeles Tuesday night. That’s the independent studio founded by “Avengers: Endgame” directors Anthony and Joe Russo. AGBO chief creative officer Angela Russo-Otstot welcomed the honorees and presented the night’s biggest award, worth $10,000.

Related Stories
ACE Eddie Awards Will Honor John Carpenter as Filmmaker of the Year
Sundance Reveals First 2027 Legacy Films for Boulder Debut: ‘Y Tu Mamá También,’ ‘Memento,’ and More

Now in its 29th year, Slamdance’s annual screenplay competition received nearly 5,000 submissions from around the world in 2026. This year’s contest recognized emerging writers across feature scripts, a dedicated horror/thriller race, TV pilots, short films, and a special screenplay mentorship category, giving out more than $18,000 in prizes. To date, the awards program reports it has distributed more than $450,000 to emerging filmmakers.

“Termite,” which also won first place in the horror/thriller competition, follows a teenager who discovers a homeless man has taken refuge in the walls of his family home. The kid lets him stay, but their bond comes with a sharp shift in the balance of power.

“’Termite’ kept us on the edge of our seats, in a way that was unmatched to any script that we read this year,” said Anna Lee Lawson, screenplay competition and festival manager, in a press release sent to IndieWire. “’Oxyer’ was inspired to write the script after he was pushed to a physical and mental breakdown to make it onto a sports team and created this thriller that embodied the rush of chasing the masculine ideal.”

Meanwhile, first place in feature went to Wes Andre Goodrich’s “Citizens.” The script follows a burned-out social studies teacher at a failing high school who must decide whether to protect a troublesome student from immigration officers or let him be taken into custody. As part of its winning package, “Citizens” will receive script coverage from Sony Pictures Classics.

Category winners receive $2,000 each, and all 12 scripts that placed in the four ranked contests will also receive legal services from Pessah Law Group, Slamdance’s official sponsor and festival legal counsel. They’ll also get one-year memberships to the industry social media platform Roadmap Writers.

Finally, Aisha Amin received the 2026 Slamdance Screenplay Stowe Fellowship, the mentorship award, for “The Redeemer.” Its story follows a grieving widow and a struggling young mom whose unlikely connection changes after a disturbing request blurs the line between closeness and control. The fellowship covers the full fee and associated benefits for attending the Stowe Story Labs Narrative Lab in Vermont. Jake Allgeier’s “Ravenous” received an honorable mention.

Read on for the complete list of the 2026 Slamdance screenplay competition winners.

entry.title: ACE Eddie Awards Will Honor John Carpenter as Filmmaker of the Year
entry.summary: Editors Bonnie Koehler, ACE, and Christopher Nelson, ACE, to receive career achievement honors.
entry.content:
The 2027 American Cinema Editors (ACE) Eddie Awards will, at least a little, be one for horror freaks. John Carpenter will receive the ACE Golden Eddie Filmmaker of the Year award. The winners will also be announced in 14 competitive categories recognizing the year’s best film editing achievements in film and television. Bonnie Koehler, ACE, and Christopher Nelson, ACE, will receive ACE Career Achievement awards.

Carpenter joins an impressive group of Golden Eddie award recipients including Ang Lee, Jon M. Chu, John Waters, Gina Prince-Bythewood, Spike Lee, Quentin Tarantino, Kathleen Kennedy, Christopher Nolan, Lauren Shuler Donner, Guillermo del Toro, Steven Spielberg, Vince Gilligan, Alexander Payne, J.J. Abrams, Nancy Meyers, Martin Scorsese, Norman Jewison, Robert Zemeckis, George Lucas, and the Sundance Institute, among many others.

Related Stories
Sundance Reveals First 2027 Legacy Films for Boulder Debut: ‘Y Tu Mamá También,’ ‘Memento,’ and More
Roberto Rossellini Retrospectives Head to New York and L.A. for the Italian Neorealist Master’s 120th Birthday

“John Carpenter makes movies that get under your skin and stay there,” said ACE president Sabrina Plisco. “‘Halloween,’ ‘The Thing,’ ‘Escape from New York’ — these films have scared, thrilled and shaped generations of audiences and filmmakers alike. Few directors understand rhythm, tension and restraint the way he does, and he has always trusted his editors to help him find it. That collaboration is exactly what this honor celebrates.”

As for the company that Koehler and Nelson are joining, past recipients of the ACE Career Achievement Award include some of the best and most beloved editors in the industry, including Arthur Forney, ACE; Robert Leighton; Maysie Hoy, ACE; Paul Hirsch, ACE; Lynne Willingham, ACE; Don Zimmerman, ACE; Lillian Benson, ACE; Richard Chew, ACE; Alan Heim, ACE; Tina Hirsch, ACE; Thelma Schoonmaker, ACE; Janet Ashikaga, ACE; Craig McKay, ACE; Jerrold L. Ludwig, ACE; Mark Goldblatt, ACE; and Leon Ortiz-Gil, ACE, among many others.

“Bonnie Koehler and Chris Nelson are editors other editors look up to,” Plisco added. “Bonnie went from American Zoetrope to an Emmy nomination for L.A. Law and an ACE Eddie nomination for ‘Law & Order: Special Victims Unit,’ television’s longest-running primetime drama. Chris cut the finale of ‘Lost,’ one of the most watched and debated hours in television history, and his work on ‘Six Feet Under’ and ‘Mad Men’ helped define prestige television. Both have given generously to our community.”

The 77th Annual ACE Eddie Awards will take place Saturday, February 6, 2027, at UCLA’s Royce Hall. Patton Oswalt, a devoted Carpenter fan and a champion of editors, returns to host the evening’s festivities and help toast one of cinema’s true originals.

Nominations for the 77th Annual ACE Eddie Awards will be announced on Thursday, January 14, 2027.

entry.title: Watermelon Pictures to Offer Discounted Tickets, Free Streaming for Gaza Doc ‘American Doctor’ Before Election Day
entry.summary: Watermelon Pictures will discount theater tickets and give a free streaming release for its Gaza documentary "American Doctor" ahead of election day.
entry.content:
Advocacy-focused Watermelon Pictures is temporarily waiving its theatrical film rental fees and box office revenue share for the documentary “American Doctor,” giving venues the option to offer discounted or free tickets.

The campaign will span roughly 50 cities and run through the week of the United States’ midterm elections, from October 30 to November 5. Watermelon hopes to expand the film’s reach to spotlight the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, which “American Doctor” documents through the perspectives of three physicians traveling to the region to provide medical aid.

In addition to discounted theatrical admissions, Watermelon is also making “American Doctor” available to stream free for one week on its streaming platform, Watermelon+, giving access to non-subscribers for a limited time. The free Watermelon+ release runs from October 30 to November 6. A video on-demand release will follow on November 10.

Related Stories
Audiences Want to See Documentaries About Gaza, Israel, and Palestine — Why Are Distributors Still Scared?
‘American Doctor’ Review: Three Doctors Travel to Gaza in a Bracing and Essential Documentary About Treating the Despair of an Ongoing Genocide

“By waiving theatrical fees and offering ‘American Doctor’ free on Watermelon+, we’re making it easier for exhibitors and audiences to access this important film during election week,” said Justin DiPietro, Watermelon’s executive VP. “At a time when the humanitarian issues it explores deserve greater attention, we want to encourage meaningful conversations and ensure this story reaches as many people as possible.”

Directed by Poh Si Teng, “American Doctor” follows three U.S.-based physicians — one Palestinian, one Jewish, and one Zoroastrian — who volunteer in Gaza to provide emergency medical care as Israel’s military attacks cripple the region’s medical infrastructure. The film earned positive reviews after its Sundance Film Festival premiere in January. IndieWire’s chief film critic David Ehrlich named “American Doctor” a Critics’ Pick in August, calling it “a bracing and essential documentary about treating the despair of an ongoing genocide.” The film has earned more than $500,000 at the domestic box office.

Watermelon previously offered complimentary screenings of “American Doctor” to healthcare workers and donated net theatrical proceeds from an entire weekend to the Palestinian American Medical Association. Founded in 2024, the distribution and production banner has handled several titles focusing on Gaza, including “From Ground Zero,” “Palestine 36” and “The Voice of Hind Rajab.”

entry.title: Sundance Reveals First 2027 Legacy Films for Boulder Debut: ‘Y Tu Mamá También,’ ‘Memento,’ and More
entry.summary: Restorations of Sundance classics like 'Nitrate Kisses' and 'Y Tu Mamá También' will screen at the festival's first Boulder edition.
entry.content:
Much of the discussion around the 2027 Sundance Film Festival has understandably focused on the festival’s move to Boulder, Colorado, from its longtime home in Park City. But with less than three months until the festival starts, it’s finally time to start discussing some films.

Sundance has announced its first wave of Legacy programming, which will screen restorations of influential films from the festival’s history in a section co-presented by Letterboxd. Highlights include Alfonso Cuarón’s “Y Tu Mamá También,” Julie Taymor’s “Fool’s Fire,” and Barbara Hammer’s landmark documentary “Nitrate Kisses,” all celebrating notable anniversaries in 2027.

Related Stories
Watch ‘Everybody to Kenmure Street’ Director Felipe Bustos Sierra Break Down the Decades of Activism That Led to One Spontaneous Protest
Jafar Panahi Faces Five-Year Prison Sentence in Iran After Releasing ‘It Was Just an Accident’

The festival will also host a special “Cinema Interruptus” screening of Christopher Nolan’s “Memento,” a University of Colorado tradition in which audience members can pause the film at any time to ask a question or spark a discussion.

“We’re excited to kick off the Festival season in earnest with this first 2027 Sundance Film Festival announcement, revealing some of our Legacy programming,” said Sundance Film Festival director Eugene Hernandez said in a statement. “Each year we honor the legacy of our founder Robert Redford and the history of the Sundance Film Festival by looking back at just a few of the films and filmmakers who have shaped our history. Our first festival in our new home in Boulder, Colorado will bring change, but as we evolve, we’ll keep at our core what we celebrate: our rich history. Sundance will always uplift independent voices, and our Legacy slate is a beautiful example of that. We are also pleased to announce Letterboxd’s co-partnership for the Legacy category — it’s great to collaborate with organizations that build momentum and excitement for a culture of cinematic discovery, and we look forward to having them at the Festival with us in January.”

The 2027 Sundance Film Festival runs from January 21-31, 2027 in Boulder, Colorado. Keep reading for the full list of announced Legacy programming, with descriptions from Sundance

“Better Luck Tomorrow” / U.S.A. (Director, Screenwriter, and Producer: Justin Lin, Screenwriters: Ernesto Foronda, Fabian Marquez, Producers: Julie Asato, Ernesto Foronda) — To escape the crushing pressure of academic perfection, a group of high-achieving teens lead a secret, thrill-seeking double life of petty crime that quickly spins out of control. Cast: Karin Anna Cheung, John Cho, Roger Fan, Sung Kang, Parry Shen, Jason Tobin. Fiction. 25th anniversary. Better Luck Tomorrow premiered at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition. It was subsequently released with small changes in the edit. The original 2002 Sundance Film Festival cut of Better Luck Tomorrow was restored by the UCLA Film & Television Archive in collaboration with Sundance Institute and Perfect Storm Entertainment, with funding provided by Chris Quintos Cathcart, co-CEO of Unapologetic Projects. The 4K restoration utilized the original 35 mm camera negatives, 35 mm Sundance Film Festival print, and DA-88 sound materials and was supervised by filmmaker Justin Lin at Resillion and Deluxe Audio Services. Additional lab services by Roundabout Entertainment, Inc. The release version has also been restored and archived. Special thanks to Paramount Pictures for permission to screen the film.


“Dogtown and Z-Boys“ / U.S.A (Director and Screenwriter: Stacy Peralta, Screenwriter: Craig Stecyk, Producer: Agi Orsi) — The Z-Boys: outcast surf rats from the run-down Dogtown neighborhood in Venice, California, who revolutionized skateboarding with their innovative style and attitude. An exploration of the birth of a cultural phenomenon, narrated by Sean Penn and featuring old-school skating footage, a blistering soundtrack, and interviews with Tony Alva, Jay Adams, and Tony Hawk. Documentary. 25th Anniversary of U.S. Release. Dogtown and Z-Boys premiered at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Documentary Competition and won the Audience Award: Documentary and Directing Award: Documentary. 2027 marks the 25th anniversary of its theatrical release. The 4K digital restoration was undertaken from the original 35 mm elements by Sony Pictures Classics. The restoration was approved by the filmmakers.

“Fool’s Fire“ / U.S.A. (Director, Screenwriter, and Producer: Julie Taymor, Producer: Kerry Orent) — A captured dwarf, Hopfrog, is forced to become jester to a tyrannical king. But when the King is gifted with another little person, whom the king debases and shames, Hopfrog plots a terrible revenge. Based on the story “Hop-Frog” by Edgar Allan Poe. Cast: Michael J. Anderson, Tom Hewitt, Mireille Mossé. Fiction. 35th anniversary. Fool’s Fire premiered at the 1992 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition. This new restoration was created by the nonprofit IndieCollect in collaboration with Julie Taymor and with support from the Golden Globe Foundation, using a 6.5K scan of the original 35 mm negative and a soundtrack restored by Endpoint Audio Labs from the optical track negative. Featuring an extended conversation with Julie Taymor and clips from The Making of Fool’s Fire, exploring the film’s artistry and cutting-edge use of high definition.

“Nitrate Kisses“ / U.S.A. (Director: Barbara Hammer) — A liberating portrait of queer sexuality that weaves striking images of four lesbian and gay couples with archival footage, interviews, sexual imagery, and queer cinema dating back to the 1930s to unearth forbidden and long-invisible histories. Documentary. Nitrate Kisses had its U.S. premiere at the 1993 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Documentary Competition. Nitrate Kisses was preserved by the Academy Film Archive. The original 16 mm A/B-rolls were scanned at 4K and restored by BB Optics. The mono mix was digitized from the original 16 mm mag track. The restoration was funded by Frameline and supervised by The Estate of Barbara Hammer and Brydie O’Connor.

“Real Women Have Curves“ / U.S.A. (Director: Patricia Cardoso, Screenwriters: George LaVoo, Josefina López, Producers: George Lavoo, Effie Brown) — Ana, a first-generation Mexican American teenager, fights for her independence and her curves in a war of wills with her mother. Based on the play by Josefina López. Cast: America Ferrera, George Lopez, Ingrid Oliu, Lupe Ontiveros, Brian Sites. Fiction. 25th anniversary. Real Women Have Curves premiered at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition and took home the Audience Award: Dramatic and the Special Jury Prize for Acting for America Ferrera and Lupe Ontiveros. Supervised by director Patricia Cardoso and director of photography Jim Denault, this new 4K restoration was undertaken by Criterion in collaboration with Warner Bros. Pictures, Sundance Institute, and the Academy Film Archive from the 35 mm original camera negative.

“Swoon“ / U.S.A. (Director and Screenwriter: Tom Kalin, Producers: Christine Vachon) — The true story of Nathan Leopold and Richard Loeb, who kidnapped and brutally murdered 14-year-old Bobby Franks in Chicago in 1924. The revelation that these wealthy Jewish college students had a sexual relationship scandalized the nation. After their arrest and trial, they were sentenced to life plus 99 years. Cast: Craig Chester, Michael Kirby, John A. Mudd, Daniel Schlachet, Natalie Stanford, Michael Stumm, Ron Vawter. Fiction. 35th anniversary. Swoon premiered at the 1992 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition and took home the Excellence in Cinematography Award: Dramatic. Swoon was restored by the Academy Film Archive and UCLA Film & Television Archive in collaboration with Frameline, Strand Releasing, and Sundance Institute in 4K from the original 16 mm A/B camera negatives, 35 mm interpositive, 35 mm dupe negative, and 35 mm magnetic track. The restoration was supervised by Tom Kalin and Ellen Kuras at Roundabout Entertainment, Inc. and Deluxe Audio Services. Restoration funding was provided by the Academy Film Archive and UCLA Film & Television Archive with additional support from Frameline, Ellen Kuras, Strand Releasing, and Sundance Institute.

“Y tu mamá también“ / Mexico (Director, Screenwriter and Producer: Alfonso Cuarón, Screenwriter: Carlos Cuarón, Producer: Jorge Vergara) — After their girlfriends jet off for the summer, a pair of Mexico City teenagers become bewitched by an older Spanish woman they meet at a wedding. When she agrees to accompany them on a road trip, the three form an increasingly intense and sensual bond. Cast: Gael García Bernal, Diego Luna, Maribel Verdú. Fiction. 25th anniversary. Y tu mamá también screened at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the Special Events category. Newly restored by Esperanto Films in 4K under the supervision of filmmaker Alfonso Cuarón and cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki. A Janus Films release.

Sundance Film Festival presents: Cinema Interruptus featuring “Memento”
A unique tradition established at the University of Colorado Boulder’s Conference on World Affairs (CWA) by film critic Roger Ebert and CWA founder and sociology professor Howard Higman, Cinema Interruptus is communal film criticism in two sessions. As “Memento” screens, participants can yell “Stop!” at any point to make a comment or ask a question, after which the film will resume. Critic and author Josh Larsen — who hosted Interruptus at CWA on campus from 2017 to 2024 — will moderate the discussion and keep things on track, with the goal of finishing the entire movie by the end of the second session.

“Memento” / U.S.A. (Director: Christopher Nolan) — A former insurance investigator who now suffers from anterograde amnesia uses notes and tattoos to hunt down his wife’s murderer. Fiction.

“Memento” had its U.S. festival premiere at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival in the U.S. Dramatic Competition and it took home the Waldo Salt Screenwriting Award. Restored in 4K from original interpositive materials by Umbrella with approval from director Christopher Nolan. Cinema Interruptus is also part of our Offscreen program, to be announced in its entirety soon.

entry.title: Roberto Rossellini Retrospectives Head to New York and L.A. for the Italian Neorealist Master’s 120th Birthday
entry.summary: Major retrospectives are headed to Film Forum and the Academy Museum in honor of Roberto Rossellini's 120th birthday.
entry.content:
Italian neorealist master Roberto Rossellini, though he died in 1977, turns 120 this year. In celebration, major retrospective series are coming up.

Film Forum in New York, the Italian Ministry of Culture, and Cinecittà will present “Rossellini 120,” a 25-film retrospective dedicated to Roberto Rossellini, opening at Film Forum on November 20. The retrospective will also open in Los Angeles on November 4 at the Academy Museum as “Roberto Rossellini Prefers Real Life,” courtesy of the Italian Ministry of Culture and Cinecittà.

Through December 10, New York’s Film Forum will host the 25-film “Rossellini 120.” The filmmaker’s daughter, Oscar-nominated actress Isabella Rossellini, will appear in person on November 20 with “Voyage to Italy” (which starred her mother, Ingrid Bergman, opposite George Sanders) and again on November 26 (i.e., Thanksgiving) with “Flowers of St. Francis” and “Europa ’51.” IndieWire shares exclusive details as well as a trailer for the retrospective above. The program is a partnership of Film Forum, Cinecittà, and the Italian Ministry of Culture

Related Stories
Watch ‘Everybody to Kenmure Street’ Director Felipe Bustos Sierra Break Down the Decades of Activism That Led to One Spontaneous Protest
Jafar Panahi Faces Five-Year Prison Sentence in Iran After Releasing ‘It Was Just an Accident’

Rossellini is best known for his films with his third wife, Ingrid Bergman, including “Stromboli,” “Europe ’51,” “Fear,” “Journey to Italy,” and “Joan of Arc at the Stake.”

Isabella said, “Our family is coming en masse to see the retrospective at Film Forum. It’s an occasion for my sister Ingrid and I to show the films to the youngest family members, who never met their Nonno (grandfather) or bisnonno (great-grandfather), in the 120th year since his birth. We’re super-grateful to both Film Forum and Cinecittà, who for years have restored and presented our father’s work. His films continue to inspire filmmakers all around the world.”

The program includes Rossellini films “Rome, Open City,” “Paisan,” “Germany, Year Zero.” The lineup also includes Guy Maddin’s “My Dad Is 100 Years Old,” featuring Isabella Rossellini, and the documentaries “Viva Ingrid!” by Alessandro Rossellini and “Rossellini Through His Own Eyes” by Adriano Aprà.

Manuela Cacciamani, CEO of Cinecittà, added, “Film Forum has long been one of New York’s most beloved homes for repertory cinema, a place where generations of audiences have discovered the great masters of world film. It is the ideal setting for the work of Roberto Rossellini, who changed the language of cinema and whose films continue to speak powerfully to our present. Cinecittà has held the rights to ten of his most representative films for thirty years, restored in our own laboratories and preserved in valuable 35mm prints, which we are delighted to make exceptionally available for this occasion, that follows the steps of many joint past initiatives, like the legendary 1993 ‘Tutto Fellini.’ We thank our U.S. partners Janus Films and The Criterion Collection for their care in distributing Rossellini’s legacy through the years”.

Film Forum audiences will also see Cinecittà’s new 4K restoration of “Fear” from 1954, which was Rossellini’s last film with Bergman. The Film Forum series arrives a couple of weeks after the launch of “Rossellini Prefers Real Life” at the Academy Museum in Los Angeles, beginning November 4. Isabella and family will also be in attendance for that series, which includes the above films for West Coasters.

entry.title: ‘The Gilded Age’ Cast on Returning for Season 4 After a Ratings Surge: ‘It’s Go Big or Go Home’
entry.summary: 'The Gilded Age' cast and creators on the scandals and relationship dramas that will come in Season 4.
entry.content:
The women of “The Gilded Age” are assembled in the lavishly appointed drawing room of the Fifth Avenue Hotel for a postmortem.

“I’m still buzzing from the other night,” Marceline Hugot, who plays Mrs. Foster, the director of the Heritage Society, says as she rises to address the group. “Despite some hiccups, President Cleveland was charmed.”

With that, the camera pulls back, and Gladys Russell (Taissa Farmiga) enters, eliciting upturned eyebrows and side glances as she makes excuses for her absent mother, Bertha Russell, whose rise to the top of society has consumed much of the HBO series’ three previous seasons. But as she begins to describe the headache that has waylaid Bertha, Farmiga’s words grow entangled, and she blows her lines.

Related Stories
‘The Gilded Age’ Review: Season 4 Is Team Bertha’s Time to Shine
James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next

“Damn it,” Farmiga exclaims, using a word that would cause any one of these ladies who lunch to stagger back toward their settee in shock.

Cut.

Farmiga grabs her script. Races through the dialogue out loud. Then exits the room to make her entrance again as a makeup artist appears to administer touch-ups and a wardrobe assistant swoops in to adjust one of the women’s hats. As fans of the show know, every detail on “The Gilded Age” has to be just right. Bringing the 19th century to life requires a small army of costumers, builders, technicians, and researchers. And Season 4, which debuts on Nov. 1, is the biggest yet. There are multiple weddings, a party at a dance hall, a parade, an inventors’ convention, the dedication of a national monument, and, yes, a presidential visit.

“Usually we have two or three events like this in a season,” said Bob Shaw, the show’s production designer. “This is the season where we keep saying, ‘it’s go big or go home.'”

The larger canvas is the reward for a ratings surge that saw “The Gilded Age,” which had languished on the bubble for its first two years, finally become appointment television. Cast members first noticed the rising interest on social media, then grew accustomed to strangers approaching them on the street to share their thoughts on Gladys’s relationship woes or George Russell’s latest corporate battle.

“It’s so rare that you let a show be on the air for a few years to find its audience,” Carrie Coon, who plays Bertha, told IndieWire. “Our attention moves on more quickly now, and I have friends on amazing shows that no one’s watching, so to know that people are actually consuming the thing you’re making is very gratifying. There’s been this uptick in people recognizing us and saying how much they love the show. It’s all over the world. It’s all socioeconomic classes. It’s every end of the political spectrum. There are fans in every corner.”

Co-creator Sonja Warfield realized “The Gilded Age” had broken through after her parents attended a funeral.

“All these people were hovering around my dad and mom,” she said. “And they didn’t want to talk about the deceased; they wanted to discuss ‘The Gilded Age.'”

There was certainly plenty for fans to unpack. After working in tandem to bring New York to heel, the Russells’ marriage came undone, with George (Morgan Spector) furious that Bertha had manipulated her daughter into marrying a duke. There was also an assassination attempt, multiple engagements, a Newport ball, and several changes in fortune (families are always rising and falling in Julian Fellowes‘ America). Online, the conversation intensified, and thirsty memes sprouted (George was dubbed “Railroad Daddy,” and Ben Ahlers’ servant-turned-inventor was christened “Clock Twink “). Warfield has a theory for why it took fans a few years to catch up with the period drama.

“Season 3 is the sweet spot for TV series,” Warfield said. “Season 1, you’re establishing the world. Season 2, you’re starting to build out the plot lines. And Season 3, the actors really know the characters and the writers know the nuances of the actors. We can write to their strengths. And that gives us more real estate for their characters’ journeys.”

For the first time, Warfield and Fellowes are entering a new season with confidence it won’t be their last. They haven’t mapped out where the Russells, the Scotts and the van Rhijns go from here, but they believe there are more stories left to tell as America enters a new age.

“We have a Season 5 in us if we’re allowed to do it,” Fellowes said. “But when you write a TV series, you have to finish every season so that it could be the end, because one day it will be.”

There’s plenty of backstabbing, social snobbery, and romantic complications to go around this season. Coon and Spector choose their words carefully, hesitant to reveal anything that flirts with being a spoiler, but they promise that the Russells’ marital problems won’t be resolved any time soon. Without his wife by his side, George, so confident in his business dealings and so adept at outmaneuvering the old-money elites whose hold on American enterprise is loosening, is unmoored. As his empire begins to teeter, he turns to dangerous ways of coping.

“George is a disaster without Bertha,” Spector said. “He’s doing everything he can to fill the void.”

Bertha is equally disoriented without her supportive spouse, but Coon believes that her character was justified in pressuring Gladys to marry royalty. The match may have been arranged, with Gladys offering wealth and the duke respectability, but as the season dawns, the couple is deeply in love. Bertha’s daughter’s future isn’t just secure — it’s bright.

“I’ve always maintained that Bertha was absolutely right,” Coon said. “She’s a good judge of character, and she really liked the Duke.”

Season 4 also promises big things for Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), the Black journalist who spent much of the first two seasons dealing with personal tragedy or bearing witness to racial violence, as she did during a trip to the South that ended with a lynch mob. But last season, Peggy fell head over heels for Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica), and the new episodes find the well-off Scott family navigating an even higher rung of Black society as they prepare for the kind of blowout wedding that the white characters are constantly attending.

“It’s wonderful to see Black joy on television,” said Audra McDonald, who plays Peggy’s mother. “We had a lot of drama and tragedy in the first couple of seasons for the Scotts, and it’s wonderful to see them emerge in this way. It’s exciting to see Peggy come out of this cocoon to become an iron butterfly.”

Then there’s Ada (Cynthia Nixon) and Agnes (Christine Baranski), who may live across the street from the Russells, but whose family line traces back to the Mayflower, making them ambassadors of the old order their new-money neighbors are threatening. Agnes once controlled the purse strings, but her wayward son Oscar (Blake Ritson) fell for a Ponzi scheme, costing them their fortune. In an only-on “The Gilded Age” coincidence, Ada came into a sizable inheritance at the exact same moment, allowing the family to retain their mansion. The role reversal comes to a head this season when Ada is expected to foot the bill for Agnes’ grand soirée for the president.

“She’s getting more comfortable with her stature, with being a woman of means, and with being the head of the household,” Nixon said.

And Baranski hints that Agnes, whose haughty putdowns are beloved by “Gilded Age” fans, gets to go in unexpected directions.

“It’s my favorite year in terms of my character’s narrative line,” she said. “I’ve never enjoyed myself more, and I’m just so grateful to the writers. Agnes’ sense of identity is challenged this season. I get to do some really powerful scenes.”

“The Gilded Age” has taken hold of the culture just as a new billionaire set is flexing their muscles. The characters on their show made their fortunes in railroads and oil, this new gang of robber barons controls everything from AI to electric cars and social networks. The parallels are hard to ignore, and some cast members seem uncomfortable lionizing rapacious capitalists while we are living through a new gilded age that seems nastier and more brutish.

“It’s so bizarre,” Nixon said. “These billionaires are the main story of our moment, and it is the main story of ‘The Gilded Age.” You have these people who appear seemingly out of nowhere and have so much money, and because of their incredible wealth and their quest for more, they are destroying everything from the planet to democracy to the Constitution, you name it.”

Fellowes acknowledges that the show romanticizes a kind of swashbuckling industrialist, but he thinks that their legacy is complicated.

“I do feel I’m sticking up for them,” Fellowes said. “If you watch a series and someone comes in who’s a millionaire from Wall Street, you know he’s the baddie. I’m a lone voice in the other direction, because I think the Gilded Age was a very exciting time for America, and these men made it exciting. They built an economy that put America at the peace table with the loudest voice in both of the coming world wars, when it had only existed as a country for one and a half centuries. I’m perfectly happy to protect people who can’t protect themselves. So I don’t want to seem as if I only support the robber barons. I don’t. But the fashion now is to hate them, and we ought to remember that they got America ready for the 20th century.”

Back on set, the cast and crew of “The Gilded Age” are entering their third hour of capturing the post-presidential visit discussion from every angle, and they’re getting punchy. Beneath their corsets, stomachs are starting to growl, and they’re eager to break for lunch. In between setups, Baranski tries to keep her energy up, scrunching her face and blowing her lips together to keep them elastic.

“This is better than a sharp stick in the eye,” Baranski tells the table as the camera crew gets ready for another shot. “I always wanted to say that while accepting an award.”

Despite the long hours (most of the actors had to arrive just after 5 a.m. to begin the hourslong process of getting in costume), “The Gilded Age” cast can’t believe that after being counted out for several seasons, they have finally, at long last, climbed to the top.

“We hope we get a fifth, a sixth, or a seventh season,” Donna Murphy, who plays Caroline Astor, said. “There’s been this gradual kind of gelling and coalescing as a company. We just keep getting better. I remember at the end of filming the third season, Christine turned to me and said, ‘I could do this for the rest of my life.’ And you know what, she’s right.”

entry.title: Watch ‘Everybody to Kenmure Street’ Director Felipe Bustos Sierra Break Down the Decades of Activism That Led to One Spontaneous Protest
entry.summary: At IndieWire's Art of the Doc event, Sierra explained why his film had to introduce Glasgow's long history of social justice protests.
entry.content:
Felipe Bustos Sierra’s “Everybody to Kenmure Street” is a powerful portrait of a neighborhood rallying around two of its own in the face of injustice. The film depicts the 2021 protests in the Pollokshields neighborhood of Glasgow, in which citizens took to the streets to protest the detention of two men for alleged immigration violations and secured their release after eight hours. But while all of the events took place in one day, Sierra understood that the film’s story began far earlier.

During a conversation with IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt at our Art of the Doc event in Los Angeles, Sierra explained why the film had to contextualize the long history of social justice activism in Glasgow. Pollokshields is the most diverse neighborhood in Scotland, with 86 languages spoken among its residents, and has always been seen as something of a safe haven for those fleeing persecution. The Kenmure Street protests might have seemed spur-of-the-moment, but in many ways they were a product of people’s connection to their city’s history.

“It came out of all these early conversations, of myself not seeing possibility or hope. When I was asking people ‘what brought you to the street?,’ ‘what actually made you take your body on the street?,’ which is what was necessary, they often talked about having no hope either. But they had that specific connection to Glasgow’s history,” Sierra said of the film’s origins.” It was always variations of fighting for women’s rights, civil rights, queer rights, housing conditions, working conditions. This shared humanity, we had to find a way to put it in the film. Of course it was a very spontaneous protest. It was the very first protest for many people who turned up. But there had been this transmission of knowledge of history, of care, and that clearly came out.”
